sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Class IV Haemorrhage: above 40% blood volume loss (hypotension + tachycardia + anuria). (2) B — 0.9% Normal Saline (isotonic crystalloid; or Hartmann's/Ringer's lactate, followed urgently by cross-matched blood/massive transfusion protocol).

domain: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 27-year-old man previously treated by a native healer presents 6 days after a snakebite passing the dark brown urine shown in the photograph. Microscopy shows 1–2 red cells/hpf, 1–2 pus cells/hpf, no casts, negative bilirubin, and negative urobilinogen, while his haemoglobin falls from 13 g/dL to 6 g/dL in 24 hours. What explains the dark urine?
options: Gross glomerular haematuria from crescentic glomerulonephritis
Cholestatic obstructive jaundice with conjugated bilirubinuria
Haemoglobinuria secondary to acute intravascular haemolysis
Extravascular haemolysis causing excess urinary urobilinogen
Acute bacterial pyelonephritis with renal papillary necrosis
optionRationales: Incorrect: True glomerular haematuria shows abundant red cells and red cell casts on urine microscopy rather than 1–2 RBCs/hpf with no casts.
Incorrect: Obstructive jaundice produces positive urinary bilirubin rather than negative urinary bilirubin and an abrupt 7 g/dL drop in haemoglobin.

Correct: Dark cola-coloured urine with an acute 7 g/dL haemoglobin drop, virtually absent red cells on microscopy (1–2 RBC/hpf), and negative bilirubin/urobilinogen confirms free haemoglobinuria from acute intravascular haemolysis (triggered by viper venom or herbal nephro-haemotoxins).
Incorrect: Extravascular haemolysis elevates urinary urobilinogen (which is negative here) and does not spill free haemoglobin into the urine.
Incorrect: Pyelonephritis causes significant pyuria and bacteriuria rather than 1–2 pus cells/hpf with catastrophic acute anaemia.
clinicalPearl: Cola-coloured urine + positive dipstick blood + virtually NO red cells on microscopy = pigmenturia (haemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria); aggressively hydrate with IV crystalloids and monitor renal function to prevent pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Viper envenoming or toxic herbal remedies can trigger acute intravascular haemolysis, presenting with steep Hb drop, dark urine, negative bilirubin, and minimal RBCs on microscopy.

sourceStation.title: Snakebite-Induced Intravascular Haemolysis (Haemoglobinuria)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
1. This is a urine sample of a 27-year-old male treated by a native physician for snakebite, 6 days after an alleged snakebite. Urine analysis:
Pus cells: 1–2/hpf | Red cells: 1–2/hpf | Casts: Nil | Bilirubin: Nil | Urobilinogen: Nil
His haemoglobin level dropped from 13 g/dL to 6 g/dL within one day.
What is the reason for dark-coloured urine?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Haemoglobinuria secondary to acute intravascular haemolysis (triggered by snake venom, e.g., Russell's viper / hump-nosed viper, or native herbal toxins; confirmed by cola/dark urine with positive dipstick blood but only 1–2 RBCs/hpf on microscopy and steep Hb drop).

domain: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 34-year-old farmer presents 12 hours after a snakebite on the dorsum of his foot with the haemorrhagic blister and local swelling shown in the photograph. Which pair of Sri Lankan snakes most characteristically produces this local bite-site appearance?
options: Common krait (Bungarus caeruleus) and Ceylon krait (Bungarus ceylonicus)
Hump-nosed viper (Hypnale hypnale) and cobra (Naja naja)
Rat snake (Ptyas mucosa) and green vine snake (Ahaetulla nasuta)
Common krait (Bungarus caeruleus) and rat snake (Ptyas mucosa)
Beaked sea snake and Ceylon krait (Bungarus ceylonicus)
optionRationales: Incorrect: Kraits typically bite sleeping victims at night and produce descending neurotoxicity with minimal or absent local swelling, pain, or blistering.

Correct: Among these Sri Lankan species, hump-nosed vipers classically produce marked local swelling, haemorrhagic blistering, and necrosis (plus AKI/coagulopathy), and cobras similarly cause severe local blistering and tissue necrosis alongside neurotoxicity.
Incorrect: The rat snake is non-venomous and the mildly venomous vine snake does not cause severe haemorrhagic blistering or tissue necrosis.
Incorrect: Neither the non-venomous rat snake nor the krait produces severe haemorrhagic blisters at the bite site.
Incorrect: Sea snakes cause rhabdomyolysis/myotoxicity and neurotoxicity with minimal local bite-site inflammation, and kraits lack local necrotic blistering.
clinicalPearl: Remember the crucial Sri Lankan clinical rule: Indian polyvalent antivenom covers Cobra, Russell's viper, Common krait, and Saw-scaled viper—it is INEFFECTIVE against Hump-nosed viper (Hypnale hypnale), which is managed supportively for local blistering, coagulopathy, and AKI.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Hump-nosed viper and cobra cause prominent local swelling and haemorrhagic blistering, whereas kraits cause severe neurotoxicity with minimal local signs.

Russell's viper also causes local blistering but wasn't listed; among the choices, Hump-nosed viper is classic for severe local haemorrhagic blisters/necrosis + AKI, and Cobra* causes local necrosis/blistering).

domain: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT (8 STATIONS)
stem: Two healthcare providers perform the resuscitation procedure shown in the photograph on an unresponsive adult with no carotid pulse and absent normal breathing. Which combination states the correct chest compression site, depth, and compression-to-ventilation ratio for adult Basic Life Support?
options: Lower half of sternum, 5–6 cm depth, 30:2 ratio
Upper half of sternum, 2–3 cm depth, 15:2 ratio
Lower half of sternum, 5–6 cm depth, 15:2 ratio
Left fifth intercostal space, 4 cm depth, 30:2 ratio
Tip of the xiphisternum, 3–4 cm depth, 5:1 ratio
optionRationales: Correct: Adult CPR with bag-valve-mask ventilation uses interlocked hands with straight arms over the lower half of the sternum, compressing 5–6 cm (about 2 inches) at 100–120/min in a 30 compressions to 2 breaths ratio.
Incorrect: Compressing the upper sternum at 2–3 cm fails to generate adequate intrathoracic cardiac output, and 15:2 applies to two-rescuer paediatric CPR rather than adults.
Incorrect: A 15:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio is used in two-rescuer paediatric resuscitation, whereas adult BLS uses 30:2 regardless of one or two rescuers prior to an advanced airway.
Incorrect: Compressions are delivered centrally over the lower half of the sternum, not laterally at the cardiac apex.
Incorrect: Pressing directly on the xiphisternum risks xiphoid fracture and hepatic laceration, and neither depth nor ratio meets adult BLS guidelines.
clinicalPearl: During two-rescuer BVM ventilation in an OSCE, hold the mask with an E-C clamp (thumb and index finger forming a C on the mask, remaining fingers lifting the mandible) and avoid hyperventilation—each breath should take 1 second just to produce visible chest rise.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Adult cardiac arrest CPR uses straight-arm compressions over the lower sternum to ~2 inches (5–6 cm) depth at a 30:2 ratio with BVM ventilation.

sourceStation.title: Cardiac Arrest — CPR & Bag-Valve-Mask Ventilation

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (4.1) Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) with Bag-Valve-Mask (BVM) ventilation. (4.2) Emergency condition: Cardiac arrest (cardiopulmonary arrest).

domain: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 20-year-old man is brought to the emergency department drowsy with pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 5 breaths/min following an alleged heroin overdose. His ABG shows pH 7.25, PaO2 98 mmHg, PaCO2 60 mmHg, and HCO3- 30 mmol/L. Which interpretation and immediate management is most appropriate?
options: Metabolic acidosis; intravenous sodium bicarbonate and flumazenil
Compensated respiratory alkalosis; high-flow oxygen via face mask alone
Mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis; urgent haemodialysis and charcoal
Acute respiratory acidosis; assisted BVM ventilation and IV naloxone
Chronic respiratory acidosis; oral acetylcysteine and non-invasive ventilation
optionRationales: Incorrect: Bicarbonate is slightly elevated rather than low, proving respiratory acidosis; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines (and risks seizures) rather than opioids.
Incorrect: A low pH of 7.25 with high PaCO2 is acidosis, not alkalosis, and high-flow oxygen without ventilatory support or naloxone fails to clear life-threatening hypercapnia.
Incorrect: Activated charcoal is contraindicated in a drowsy patient without a secured airway, and heroin toxicity is reversed specifically by naloxone rather than dialysis.

Correct: Marked hypoventilation (RR 5/min) raises PaCO2 to 60 mmHg and drops pH to 7.25, representing acute respiratory acidosis from opioid toxicity; immediate management is airway/BVM ventilation with O2 plus titrated IV naloxone (monitoring closely for re-sedation as naloxone wears off faster than heroin).
Incorrect: The minimal bicarbonate rise relative to PaCO2 60 mmHg indicates acute hypoventilation, and acetylcysteine treats paracetamol poisoning rather than opioid overdose.
clinicalPearl: Never discharge or leave a heroin-overdose patient unmonitored after a single IV naloxone bolus: naloxone's half-life (30–60 min) is shorter than many opioids, so recurrent respiratory depression frequently develops.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Opioid-induced hypoventilation causes acute respiratory acidosis (low pH, high PaCO2); secure airway/BVM ventilation and administer titrated IV naloxone while watching for re-sedation.

sourceStation.title: Heroin Overdose — Acute Respiratory Acidosis & Management
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
18. A 20-year-old boy was admitted due to overdose of heroin. He was drowsy. Respiratory rate was 5/min. Arterial blood gas findings:
pH: 7.25 | PO2: 98 mmHg | PCO2: 60 mmHg | HCO3-: 30 mmol/L (24–29)
18.1 What is the abnormality in the blood gas findings?
18.2 What is the immediate management to correct the abnormality?  [Text-only ABG station]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (18.1) Acute (uncompensated/partially compensated) respiratory acidosis due to opioid-induced central hypoventilation (low pH, markedly elevated PCO₂). (18.2) Immediate management: (a) Airway & breathing support (jaw thrust/airway adjunct, assisted BVM ventilation with O₂); (b) IV Naloxone (0.4–2 mg IV, titrated to restore adequate respiratory effort; monitor closely for re-sedation because naloxone half-life is shorter than heroin).

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
topic: Blood Gas Analysis — PaO2/FiO2 Ratio & Inspired Oxygen
stem: A 35-year-old man admitted with dyspnoea following a stab injury to the chest has an arterial blood gas showing pH 7.48, PaO2 90 mmHg, and PaCO2 32 mmHg. Which additional parameter is essential to interpret this PaO2 value and accurately quantify impaired oxygenation?
options: Serum haemoglobin concentration to calculate total arterial oxygen content
Inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) to calculate the PaO2/FiO2 ratio
Standard bicarbonate level to evaluate acute respiratory alkalosis compensation
Central venous oxygen saturation to determine tissue oxygen extraction
Alveolar minute ventilation to assess carbon dioxide clearance capacity
optionRationales: Incorrect: Although haemoglobin determines total blood oxygen-carrying capacity, PaO2 reflects dissolved plasma oxygen tension driven by alveolar-capillary transfer relative to inspired FiO2, not haemoglobin concentration.

Correct: Arterial PaO2 cannot be interpreted in isolation; dividing PaO2 by FiO2 (for example, PaO2 90 mmHg on FiO2 0.50 yields a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 180 mmHg, compared with 450 mmHg on room air) is essential to quantify gas-exchange impairment and shunt.

Incorrect: Standard bicarbonate evaluates the non-respiratory (metabolic) acid-base component (which explains his mild alkalotic pH 7.48 from hyperventilation to PaCO2 32 mmHg), rather than quantifying pulmonary oxygenation.
Incorrect: Central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) from a VBG assesses global systemic oxygen supply-to-demand balance rather than quantifying alveolar oxygenation efficiency on an ABG.
Incorrect: Minute ventilation governs PaCO2 elimination (ventilation), whereas quantifying impaired oxygen transfer requires relating arterial PaO2 to the inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2).
clinicalPearl: Per the Kelaniya Blood Gas Analysis guide, never label a PaO2 of 90–100 mmHg as normal without checking FiO2: calculate the PaO2/FiO2 ratio (normal >400 mmHg; <=300 mmHg indicates impaired gas exchange) and recognise that PaO2 90 mmHg on FiO2 0.50 equals a P/F ratio of 180 mmHg.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Quantifying oxygenation on an ABG requires factoring in inspired FiO2 (via the PaO2/FiO2 ratio) rather than interpreting PaO2 in isolation.

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Ulnar Paradox in Peripheral Nerve Palsies
stem: A 28-year-old woman sustains a deep laceration across the medial anterior wrist, developing marked clawing of the ring and little fingers with MCP hyperextension and IP flexion. Compared with a complete ulnar nerve lesion at the elbow, why is the claw-hand deformity more pronounced in this distal wrist injury?
options: The extensor digitorum communis and extensor indicis are denervated at the wrist
All four lumbrical muscles are spared when the nerve is cut proximal to Guyon's canal
The palmar interossei receive dual innervation from the anterior interosseous nerve
The flexor carpi ulnaris pulls the proximal phalanges into hyperextension
The medial half of flexor digitorum profundus remains intact to flex the DIP joints
optionRationales: Incorrect: Digital extensors are innervated proximally in the forearm by the posterior interosseous branch of the radial nerve, not the ulnar nerve at the wrist.
Incorrect: The ulnar nerve supplies the third and fourth lumbricals distally in the hand, so they are paralysed in both wrist and elbow lesions.
Incorrect: All palmar and dorsal interossei are innervated exclusively by the deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve.
Incorrect: Flexor carpi ulnaris inserts onto the pisiform/fifth metacarpal base to flex and adduct the wrist, without extending the MCP joints.

Correct: In the 'ulnar paradox', a wrist lesion spares the proximal ulnar branches in the forearm to the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (FDP), so unopposed FDP pulls the interphalangeal joints into exaggerated flexion when the medial lumbricals are paralysed.
clinicalPearl: Always remember the 'ulnar paradox' in Neurology OSCE stations: distal ulnar nerve lesions at the wrist produce uglier, more severe clawing of digits 4–5 than proximal lesions at the elbow because FDP remains intact.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Ulnar paradox: a wrist lesion causes worse clawing than an elbow lesion because proximal innervation to the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus is preserved.

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Retina & Fundoscopy — Central Retinal Vein Occlusion
stem: A 64-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension and primary open-angle glaucoma develops sudden, painless unilateral visual loss in his right eye. Direct ophthalmoscopy reveals disc hyperaemia, markedly engorged tortuous retinal veins, and widespread haemorrhages radiating across all four quadrants ('stormy sunset' appearance). What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Central retinal vein occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Primary glaucomatous optic atrophy
Dry age-related macular degeneration
optionRationales: Correct: Sudden painless visual loss with severely engorged tortuous veins and diffuse four-quadrant retinal haemorrhages ('stormy sunset' fundus) is the textbook presentation of central retinal vein occlusion, classically linked with hypertension and glaucoma.

Incorrect: Central retinal artery occlusion produces a pale, ischaemic retina with attenuated arteries and a central 'cherry-red spot' at the fovea rather than diffuse four-quadrant venous haemorrhages.

Incorrect: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is characterised by fragile new vessel formation (neovascularisation at the disc or elsewhere) rather than acute unilateral four-quadrant venous engorgement.
Incorrect: Advanced glaucoma produces gradual peripheral field loss with a pale, widened, deeply excavated optic cup rather than sudden haemorrhagic engorgement.
Incorrect: Dry macular degeneration causes gradual central visual distortion with choroidal drusen and macular pigment changes rather than acute diffuse retinal haemorrhages.
clinicalPearl: Know the iconic Kelaniya Retina OSCE spotter descriptors: CRVO = 'stormy sunset' engorged veins and haemorrhages; malignant hypertensive retinopathy = 'star-burst' macular exudates + papilloedema; CRAO = pale retina + cherry-red spot.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Central retinal vein occlusion shows a 'stormy sunset' fundus with engorged tortuous veins and extensive accompanying retinal haemorrhages.

stem: A 44-year-old man with obesity presents with asymptomatic, well-demarcated reddish-brown scaly plaques in both groins and axillae. A fungal scraping for hyphae is negative, and Wood's ultraviolet light examination demonstrates bright coral-red fluorescence. Which organism is responsible for this infection?
options: Trichophyton rubrum
Malassezia furfur
Candida albicans
Corynebacterium minutissimum
Streptococcus pyogenes
optionRationales: Incorrect: Tinea cruris due to Trichophyton rubrum shows branching hyphae on KOH microscopy, an active raised scaly border with central clearing, and no coral-red Wood's light fluorescence.
Incorrect: Pityriasis versicolor caused by Malassezia furfur affects the upper trunk and exhibits pale yellow-green fluorescence under Wood's light rather than coral-red flexural plaques.
Incorrect: Candidal intertrigo produces bright beefy-red macerated plaques with satellite pustules and does not fluoresce coral-red on Wood's lamp examination.

Correct: Erythrasma is a superficial bacterial skin-fold infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum; bacterial coproporphyrin III production causes characteristic coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp.
Incorrect: Erysipelas due to beta-haemolytic streptococci causes acute painful, febrile, raised erythematous plaques rather than indolent brown scaly plaques with porphyrin fluorescence.
clinicalPearl: In the Kelaniya Bone & Skin Infections guide, differentiate groin/axillary plaques rapidly using Wood's light: coral-red fluorescence confirms Corynebacterium minutissimum erythrasma (treated with topical/oral erythromycin or fusidic acid) rather than tinea.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Erythrasma (Corynebacterium minutissimum) forms well-defined reddish-brown flexural plaques exhibiting coral-red Wood's lamp fluorescence from porphyrins.

domain: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 32-year-old paddy farmer is bitten on the right ankle by a viper while working in the field and arrives at a rural clinic 15 minutes later. Which immediate pre-hospital first-aid action is recommended by the Emergency Medicine OSCE protocol prior to urgent hospital transfer?
options: Apply a tight proximal arterial tourniquet above the right knee
Make shallow cruciform incisions over the fang marks to drain venom
Remove tight ornaments, immobilise the limb, and transfer urgently
Pack the bitten foot in crushed ice to slow systemic venom spread
Administer intramuscular adrenaline prophylactically before transfer
optionRationales: Incorrect: Arterial tourniquets are strictly contraindicated because they exacerbate local ischaemic necrosis and can precipitate sudden systemic venom bolus release upon removal.
Incorrect: Incising or sucking the bite wound is ineffective and risks severe bleeding in viper-induced coagulopathy alongside secondary wound infection.

Correct: Emergency Medicine CSS protocol mandates removing rings, anklets, and tight clothing (before swelling progresses), gently cleansing with soap and water if soiled, immobilising the bitten limb, and transferring to hospital ASAP.
Incorrect: Cryotherapy with ice packs worsens local tissue ischaemia and necrosis without reducing systemic envenoming.
Incorrect: Adrenaline is reserved for treating acute anaphylaxis (for example, reactions to antivenom) rather than routine initial snakebite first aid.
clinicalPearl: Kelaniya Emergency Medicine OSCE 'Should Do / Should Not Do' checklist for snakebites: DO remove ornaments, reassure, immobilise, and get to hospital ASAP; DO NOT apply tourniquets or make incisions.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Immediate snakebite first aid: remove tight ornaments, cleanse gently, immobilise the limb, and transfer to hospital ASAP; never apply tourniquets or incise the wound.

stem: A 35-year-old man with acute watery diarrhoea and mild dehydration is prescribed WHO reduced-osmolarity Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS), prepared by dissolving one 20.5 g packet in 1 litre of clean drinking water. Which statement accurately describes its osmolarity and physiological action?
options: Total osmolarity is 311 mmol/L; hypertonic glucose draws water passively into the gut lumen
Total osmolarity is 245 mmol/L; sodium bicarbonate prevents hypokalaemic paralytic ileus
Total osmolarity is 150 mmol/L; potassium chloride directly neutralises bacterial enterotoxins
Total osmolarity is 330 mmol/L; active chloride secretion drives intestinal water absorption
Total osmolarity is 245 mmol/L; Na+-glucose co-transport stays intact and citrate corrects acidosis
optionRationales: Incorrect: The older 311 mmol/L formulation was replaced by 245 mmol/L ORS precisely to reduce osmotic diarrhoea, and water follows sodium-glucose absorption out of the lumen into enterocytes.
Incorrect: Modern WHO ORS uses trisodium citrate dihydrate (rather than bicarbonate, for longer shelf stability) to treat acidosis, while potassium chloride prevents hypokalaemic ileus.
Incorrect: Total osmolarity is 245 mmol/L (not 150 mmol/L), and potassium chloride replaces faecal potassium losses rather than neutralising toxins.
Incorrect: Active chloride secretion (as triggered by cholera toxin via cAMP) causes secretory fluid loss; ORS works via intact glucose-coupled sodium absorption.

Correct: WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS (245 mmol/L: Na+ 75, glucose 75, Cl- 65, K+ 20, citrate 10 mmol/L) relies on coupled Na+-glucose co-transport (SGLT1), which remains intact even during enteritis, while KCl prevents hypokalaemia and trisodium citrate corrects metabolic acidosis.
clinicalPearl: Know the exact Kelaniya ORS OSCE numbers: 1 packet (20.5 g) in 1 L clean drinking water gives 245 mmol/L (Na+ 75, glucose 75, K+ 20, Cl- 65, citrate 10 mmol/L); discard unused solution after 24 hours, and switch to IV fluids if altered mental status, ileus, or persistent vomiting prevents oral intake.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Reduced-osmolarity WHO ORS (245 mmol/L; 20.5 g/L) exploits intact Na+-glucose co-transport, provides K+ (20 mmol/L) against hypokalaemia, and uses trisodium citrate (10 mmol/L) to correct acidosis.
